**On Lichen**

Consider the lichen. It has no right to exist, really—a fungus and an alga (or sometimes a cyanobacterium) locked in a partnership so intimate that for centuries we mistook them for a single organism. Even now, biologists argue about what to call it. Some insist it isn't one thing at all but a miniature ecosystem wearing a coat.

Lichen grows where almost nothing else will. Bare rock after a glacier retreats. The roof of an abandoned barn. A gravestone in a churchyard, slowly being converted back into soil, letter by letter. It doesn't rush. Some colonies grow less than a millimeter per year, which means the map of orange crusts on that boulder might be older than the language you're reading this in.

There's something instructive in that slowness. We live in a culture obsessed with growth metrics, with scaling, with disruption. Lichen disrupts nothing. It persists—photosynthesizing patiently through its algal partner, pulling minerals from stone, surviving drought by essentially shutting down and reviving with each rainfall. Scientists once exposed lichen to the vacuum of space for fifteen days; when they brought it home, it resumed photosynthesis as if nothing had happened.

Maybe that's the quiet lesson: resilience isn't always dramatic. Sometimes it looks like showing up on bare rock, decade after decade, doing the unglamorous work of turning stone into garden. No applause, no milestones, no quarterly reports. Just green-gray patience, spreading across the hardest surfaces of the world, proving that life doesn't need ideal conditions—it only needs enough of a foothold, and time.
